covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832.

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000a.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('3.50×10² milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('9.05×10² milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: meteoritic (CI-chondrite) value; unc = 1 sigma in dex as printed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.reference: Rettig, S. J.; Trotter, J. (1987). Acta Crystallographica, Section C 43, 2260.
crystal.note: α-S8 at 298 K. COD 9011363 is the same paper's high-angle refinement. Space-group origin choice 2 as in the CIF.

production.basis: production, sulfur in all forms, sulfur content

tonnesPerYear.note: World production, sulfur in all forms, sulfur content, 2025 (USGS: 84,000 thousand metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average unit value, free on board, mine and (or) plant, dollars per metric ton of elemental sulfur [Sulfur], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.100, massive_stars 0.613, white_dwarfs 0.288); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 81 px. Cross-check with the paper's text: '29% of S ... come from SNe Ia' (figure reading 0.288). Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

bonding.note: Crowns of eight atoms, S₈, in the common yellow forms; many other rings and chains exist.

air.text: Stable in air at room temperature; burns with a blue flame to sulfur dioxide when lit.

water.text: Insoluble in water and does not react with it.

acids.text: Not attacked by non-oxidising acids; hot concentrated nitric or sulfuric acid oxidise it.

plantRole.text: Taken up as sulfate; part of the amino acids cysteine and methionine, of glutathione and of iron–sulfur clusters.

humanRole.text: Part of the amino acids methionine and cysteine; obtained from dietary protein.

history.nameOrigin: From the Latin sulfur (also spelled sulphur), the Romans' name for the substance.
history.note: Known since prehistory as brimstone. Jefferson Lab credits Lavoisier with persuading chemists around 1777 that it is an element; CIAAW credits Gay-Lussac and Thénard with proving it in 1809.

prose.text: Sulfur is a bright-yellow nonmetal, the 'brimstone' of old texts, found around volcanic vents and in large underground deposits; it is an essential part of proteins and of the sharp garlic and mustard compounds that plants make to defend themselves. Pure sulfur hardly smells; the rotten-egg odour belongs to hydrogen sulfide. Melted, it is a runny yellow liquid, but heated further it suddenly turns dark red and as thick as treacle, because its eight-atom rings break open and link into long chains. The atom, [Ne] 3s² 3p⁴ (ground term ³P₂), has two unpaired 3p electrons, and nature provides four stable isotopes, mostly sulfur-32.
